Best Games for 6+ Players: 5 That Survive Big Game Night

2026-09-21

My first 6+ game night was a disaster. I grabbed the games everyone knows. Monopoly, then Pictionary. Monopoly lasted 40 minutes before two people stopped talking to each other. Pictionary had one guy sketching a horse for five minutes while the whole room yelled. We never finished a single game.

The problem was not the people. It was the games. Most games are built for 4 players. Throw in a sixth or eighth person and they fall apart. People sit out. Rounds drag. The quiet ones stop being part of it. That is the real test, and most games fail it.

I have run a game night every week for two years now, usually with 6 to 9 people. Here are the 5 games that actually survived. The ones where everybody stays busy, nobody gets benched, and the night ends with people asking to play again.

What a 6+ Game Needs. And What Kills It.

Here is the key insight: a big group game has exactly two jobs. First, every player has something to do every turn. Second, it ends before people get bored. A game that nails those two beats wins. A game that does not, no matter how smart, dies at the table.

The killer is downtime. In a 4-player strategy game, you wait your turn and it comes fast. Double the people and you wait five minutes between turns. That is the death of a big game night. The best 6+ games solve this by doing the opposite: they make you work during other people's turns, watching, predicting, or drawing.

Think about a full table of 8. There is no room for a big board. There is no patience for a 90 minute slog. What you need is something fast, loud, and cooperative enough that nobody feels picked on. Everything below leans on that.

1. Telestrations. The Drawing Game That Needs Zero Talent.

Telestrations is telephone, but with drawings. Everyone gets a little book. Everyone starts with a secret word. You draw it, pass the book, the next person guesses what your drawing is, writes it down, passes again, the next person draws that guess, and so on around the whole circle. When the book comes back to you, you reveal what everyone drew.

I have played this with a group where two people flat out said "I can't draw." They were the ones laughing hardest by round three. Terrible drawing is the whole point. Someone draws a basketball as a lumpy brown square, the next person guesses "potato," and then someone has to draw a potato, which becomes "beach ball." By the end, a $3 word like "chair" has traveled the whole table and come back as "large prehistoric bird."

This is the best big-group icebreaker I own. Every player is drawing at the same time, so nobody sits out. Nobody gets singled out, because the paper does the work, not the person. It handles players who are terrible artists and players who are shy. It is $24.99 and plays 4 to 6 players out of the box, with an 8-player pack if your table is packed.

However, there is a cost. Telestrations is not a thinking game. It is a laughing game. If your group wants strategy and tight competition, this is the wrong pick. Bring it out when you want the room in stitches, not when you want a real contest.

2. Herd Mentality. The One Where Copying Is the Goal.

Herd Mentality flips party games on their head. Normally you want to be clever. Here, you want to be boring. Someone reads a prompt like "Name a fruit." Everyone secretly writes an answer. If your answer matches the majority, you score. If yours is unique, you get nothing, and you take the pink cow token that loses you points the next round.

I have watched a grown adult freeze over "name a sport" for a full minute, terrified someone else would pick the same one as his first choice. That is the game. It fills a table up to 20 players, which is more than any other game on this list. For big groups, that alone makes it worth owning.

Here is why that matters. Most big-group games need you to perform, to draw or act or speak. Herd Mentality needs none of that. It just needs everyone to think like everyone else. Quiet beginners can win. The game runs 20 minutes and costs $24.99. The only risk is a table full of contrarians. If everybody refuses to agree, nobody scores and it falls flat.

Here is the part I did not expect: The game my group requests most at 8 players is not the smartest or the most expensive. It is Telestrations at $24.99. Price does not predict how well a game survives a big table. I have watched $50 games flop with 6 people and cheap ones carry the whole night. For 6+ players, the game that keeps everyone busy beats everything else, including the one with the best components.

3. Wavelength. The Game That Starts Arguments.

Wavelength is a spectrum game. A dial sits between two extremes. "Hot to Cold." "Easy to Hard." One player sees a hidden target and gives a one-word clue. The team guesses where the target sits on the scale. The closer you get, the more you score.

This is the game that makes a big group talk. We had a room of 8 arguing for ten minutes about where "ketchup" sits on the spectrum "Good Condiment to Bad Condiment." Somebody said the target was near the high end. Half the table swore it was in the middle. The tension is real because there is no right answer, only a guess about what your teammate thinks.

Wavelength plays 4 to 8 and runs about 30 minutes at $32. It works best when your group is already warmed up and debating. But it needs at least one confident player per team to lead the guess. If your whole table is shy and quiet, it can stall. Pair it after an icebreaker like Telestrations and it shines.

4. Sequence. The Classic That Scales to 12.

Sequence is the quiet one on this list, and sometimes that is exactly what a big night needs. It blends cards with a board. Play a card, place a chip, try to get five in a row. It handles up to 12 players, split into teams, which keeps the board clear and the tension high.

The reason it survives big groups is the teams. With 8 or 12 players you divide into two, so you are always watching your teammates' cards and planning together. Nobody is glued to a phone waiting for a turn. That is the job of a big group game, and Sequence does it better than most.

It is the oldest game here, proven for 40 years, and costs $19.97. Every age plays it. The catch: it is not a laugh out loud game. It is calm and strategic. I keep it in the rotation for when the party needs a breather between the loud drawing games.

5. Mysterium. The Co-op Mystery for a Full Table.

Mysterium is cooperative, so the whole table works together instead of fighting. One player is a ghost who communicates by handing out surreal dream cards. The rest are psychics trying to solve a murder. No one gets eliminated, which matters a lot at a big table where you want everyone included to the end.

Mysterium plays 2 to 7 and runs about 45 minutes. It is the slowest and heaviest game here, at $47.99. I would not start a night with it. But when a 6 or 7 person group wants something with more weight than a party game, it is the best co-op choice. Nobody sits out, everybody reads the weird art, and the ghost always creates a ridiculous debate about what a purple face with a key in its mouth means.

Here is the honest part. Mysterium needs a confident ghost. If that player is new, the game can bog down. Pick it when your table is warmed up and at least one person knows the rules.

How to Pick the Right One for Your Big Group

The full table needs a plan, not a single game. Here is how I run my night.

Start with Telestrations to break the ice. It gets every stranger drawing and laughing within minutes, and it is impossible to do badly. Then move to something argumentative like Wavelength once the room is loud. If the group skews calm or older, swap in Sequence instead, it keeps people thinking without pressure.

Use Herd Mentality when you have a huge crowd of 8, 10, or 12 and want pure silly fun. Keep Mysterium as the heavy closer for when a smaller subgroup wants to keep going with something deeper. That rotation has carried me through two years of weekly game nights with 6 to 9 people, and I have stopped guessing. I reach for these five first, every time.

Most of these hover in the same $20 to $32 band and bounce around on Amazon. If you buy one for a big group, start with Telestrations, it is the safest first buy and the one that surprises people most. Then add Herd Mentality for big crowds.
